Teoh Jiun Ee, Chief Executive Officer of CARSOME Academy and Co-founder of CARSOME Group, at CARSOME Academy’s 5th anniversary celebration and first graduation ceremony, shared that since 2021, 593 students have registered with the Academy, with 90% securing employment within three months. The Academy has also trained more than 8,000 employees, developed over 500 leaders and supported 280 scholarship recipients.  “Now, we are taking that further. By expanding into automotive sales and working with partners such as Maybank Islamic and JETOUR, we are connecting more people to the skills, experience and opportunities they need to succeed. As we look to the next five years, our ambition is to keep building a stronger, more future-ready automotive workforce,” he added.  The new programmes mark the Academy’s continued expansion beyond technical training, opening up recognised opportunities in automotive sales while helping employers develop job-ready talent. As it enters its next five years, CARSOME Academy will continue strengthening training and employment initiatives across the automotive ecosystem, connecting people, skills and opportunity to the industry’s evolving talent needs.  Distinguished guests and industry partners join CARSOME Academy in commemorating its 5th anniversary and celebrating the achievements of its graduating students. From L-R: ● Puan Siti Kamariah Ahmad Sukri, Pengarah Urusan Yayasan Hasanah ● Mohamad Yasin Abdullah, CEO, Maybank Islamic Berhad ● Nicholas Ng, Vice President, Jetour Malaysia  ● Y.B. Tuan Mohd Najwan Bin Halimi, Selangor State Exco for Youth, Sports, and Entrepreneurship ● Teoh Jiun Ee, CARSOME Co-Founder & Chief Executive Officer of CARSOME Academy ● Eric Cheng, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer of CARSOME ● Ts. Dr. Wan Nasarudin Bin Wan Jalal, Pengarah Jabatan Pembangunan Kemahiran Wilayah Tengah  For more information please visit CARSOME Academy’s website.  About CARSOME Academy  CARSOME Academy is the automotive education arm of CARSOME and one of Southeast Asia’s leading accredited training institutions for future automotive talent. Accredited by the Department of Skills Development (DSD) and recognised as an HRD Corp training provider, CARSOME Academy offers Malaysian Skills Certificate (SKM) programmes in Automotive Technology and a variety of upskilling opportunities to support talent development in the automotive sector.  Since its establishment in 2021, CARSOME Academy has trained more than 8,000 students and achieved a 95% job placement rate within three months. Beyond classroom training, CARSOME Academy emphasises holistic development by equipping learners with both technical expertise and essential soft skills to prepare them for long-term success in the automotive industry.  Through collaborations with foundations, government agencies, and community organisations, CARSOME Academy supports accessible education for B40 and underserved communities, with over 90% graduates coming from these backgrounds. By developing skilled, future-ready professionals, CARSOME Academy continues to strengthen the region’s automotive ecosystem.  CARSOME is Southeast Asia’s largest integrated car e-commerce platform. With operations across Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Singapore, CARSOME aims to digitize the region’s used car industry by reshaping and elevating the car transaction and ownership experience.

title: How should FIs build and sustain digital trust when AI is transforming the threat landscape?
body: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become one of the defining technologies shaping the future of financial services. Banks are embedding AI into customer service, credit assessment, payments, fraud detection, wealth management, software development and internal operations at an unprecedented pace. The rapid emergence of generative AI (Gen AI) and increasingly autonomous AI agents has further accelerated adoption, bringing forward productivity gains that many institutions had previously expected only later in the decade. The same technologies, however, are simultaneously transforming the threat landscape. Cybercriminals are using AI to automate reconnaissance, personalise phishing attacks, generate convincing deepfakes and industrialise fraud at a scale that was previously impossible. Financial institutions therefore find themselves competing in an environment where both defenders and attackers increasingly rely on the same technological capabilities. This convergence is changing the nature of cybersecurity itself. Security can no longer be treated as a specialised technology function operating alongside the business. Instead, it has become intertwined with AI governance, enterprise risk management, data governance, operational resilience and board oversight. Decisions about AI deployment increasingly have implications not only for efficiency and customer experience but also for regulatory compliance, institutional trust and financial stability. Regulators worldwide have largely moved beyond asking whether financial institutions should adopt AI. Instead, the emphasis has shifted towards how institutions can deploy AI safely, transparently and accountably while maintaining public confidence in financial services. In this environment, digital trust increasingly becomes the outcome of disciplined governance rather than technological sophistication alone. The new generation of intelligent threats AI is altering the economics of cybercrime. Many attacks that previously required significant technical expertise, manual preparation and considerable time can now be executed more quickly, at greater scale and with far higher levels of personalisation. The challenge facing financial institutions is therefore no longer confined to defending against isolated attacks but responding to an increasingly adaptive threat ecosystem. Industry evidence increasingly supports this shift. The World Economic Forum (WEF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and leading cyber-security researchers have all warned that Gen AI is reducing the cost of fraud, increasing the speed of attack and enabling highly personalised social engineering campaigns. The result is that institutions now face adversaries capable of operating with levels of automation previously available only to large organisations. On AI-driven fraud, Raad Khraishi, Head of AI Research and Development, NatWest Group, observed that AI is dramatically reducing the cost of personalisation for criminals. Publicly available information, breached data and AI-powered research tools allow attackers to construct highly targeted social engineering campaigns automatically. Combined with advances in voice synthesis, image generation and deepfake technologies, fraud can now exploit both digital identities and human trust with far greater sophistication than before. The significance is not simply that attacks are becoming more sophisticated. Rather, AI is collapsing the traditional asymmetry between attack and defence. Defensive controls are still deployed through structured governance, procurement and regulatory oversight, while attackers can iterate continuously at machine speed. The challenge for financial institutions is therefore organisational as much as technological. The implications extend beyond individual scams. Rather than relying on single exploits, attackers increasingly combine multiple vulnerabilities across identity systems, software supply chains and human behaviour. This evolution makes fraud detection considerably more difficult because institutions must identify coordinated attack patterns rather than isolated malicious events. Deepfake technologies illustrate how rapidly this threat environment is evolving. Fraud no longer begins with the transaction itself. Instead, it often originates at the identity layer, where convincing synthetic voices, videos and documents are used to manipulate customers, employees or counterparties before financial transactions even occur. These attacks exploit confidence in familiar identities rather than weaknesses in banking systems alone. AI is creating opportunities for defenders as well as attackers. Behavioural analytics, continuous authentication and AI-assisted monitoring can identify anomalies that traditional rules-based systems frequently miss. David Ng, Group Head of IT Security, Maybank pointed to behavioural biometrics as one area likely to become increasingly important. Rather than relying solely on passwords or physical biometrics, future authentication may increasingly consider behavioural characteristics such as typing rhythm, mouse movements and interaction patterns as additional indicators of identity. Raad Khraishi, Head of AI Research and Development, NatWest Group David Ng, Group Head of IT Security, Maybank The wider cybersecurity ecosystem is already responding through greater investment in behavioural analytics, digital identity, AI-enabled monitoring and cross-sector collaboration. Rather than representing isolated technological threats, these developments reinforce the growing need for integrated cyber resilience, stronger identity assurance and closer collaboration across the financial ecosystem. Building enterprise-wide digital trust As AI becomes embedded across banking operations, governance is emerging as the primary determinant of whether institutions can deploy intelligent systems at scale without compromising trust. The discussion has therefore shifted beyond cybersecurity in its traditional sense towards the broader question of how banks govern AI throughout its lifecycle. This requires institutions to manage not only technology risks but also accountability, explainability, operational resilience and regulatory compliance within a single enterprise-wide framework. The greatest risk today is not AI itself but the manner in which it is being introduced into organisations. Dee Lawler, Chief Technology Officer, Global Financial Services and Insurance Sector, International Markets, Atos, described AI as entering enterprise environments “by stealth”, through software upgrades, embedded copilots and vendor products that incorporate AI functionality without always being subject to the same governance disciplines applied to conventional technology deployments. In regulated industries such as banking, she argued that institutions would never deploy production systems without testing, validation, observability and security controls, yet AI capabilities are increasingly appearing across enterprise technology estates without equivalent scrutiny. This observation reflects one of the industry’s emerging governance challenges. Traditional technology governance was designed around deterministic systems whose outputs could be predicted and validated. Gen AI fundamentally changes that assumption. Models evolve, generate probabilistic responses and increasingly interact autonomously with other systems through AI agents. Governance therefore becomes a continuous operational discipline rather than a project approval process conducted before deployment. This represents a significant departure from traditional technology governance. Conventional governance assumes software behaves predictably once tested and deployed. AI systems, particularly foundation models and autonomous agents, require continuous supervision because their behaviour depends not only on software but also on evolving data, prompts, interactions and operating context. Governance therefore becomes an operational capability rather than a compliance checkpoint. Lawler argued that organisations need to move beyond conventional governance mechanisms such as periodic steering committees and manual approvals towards what she described as “governance as code”, where automated supervisory controls continuously monitor AI behaviour, constrain agent activity and verify compliance in real time. Rather than governing individual applications, institutions increasingly need governance architectures capable of supervising machine decision-making across interconnected AI ecosystems. Enterprise visibility is becoming increasingly important. As AI capabilities become embedded across software platforms, many organisations no longer have a complete inventory of where AI is operating or what decisions it influences. This creates governance blind spots that extend beyond cybersecurity into compliance, operational resilience and third-party risk management. For Randall Duran, Senior Lecturer at Singapore Management University, the challenge is compounded by the pace of technological change. While institutions are attempting to define their long-term AI strategies, they cannot reliably predict what banking will look like by 2030. Rather than attempting to optimise for a single future, he argued that banks should build adaptable organisational capabilities that allow them to respond to multiple possible technology trajectories. Governance therefore becomes less about constraining innovation than enabling institutions to innovate safely despite uncertainty. Dee Lawler, Chief Technology Officer, Global Financial Services and Insurance Sector, International Markets, Atos Randall Duran, Senior Lecturer at Singapore Management University There is a growing challenge to the assumption that every operational problem requires an AI solution. Lawler cautioned against deploying AI simply because it is available, arguing that some longstanding banking processes should instead be redesigned or eliminated altogether. Automation, robotic process automation, machine learning or business process re-engineering may in many cases deliver better outcomes than introducing Gen AI into unsuitable workflows. The objective should therefore be optimisation based on business value rather than technology novelty. This pragmatic approach was reinforced by Balaji Rajagopalan, Chief Technology Officer, State Bank of India, who consistently framed AI adoption around measurable operational outcomes rather than technical sophistication. He cited examples where AI reduced document scrutiny processes for trade finance and guarantees from several hours to minutes by identifying exceptions, anomalies and rule breaches automatically. For him, value creation begins with removing repetitive work, improving productivity and allowing employees to focus on higher-value activities rather than replacing human judgement altogether. Customer-facing AI should similarly improve contextual service by providing continuity across digital channels while supporting faster decisions and more personalised interactions. These operational discussions increasingly intersect with regulatory expectations. Financial regulators outlined broadly similar principles despite differences in national approaches. Rather than prescribing detailed technical requirements, each emphasised governance, accountability and proportionality as the foundations of responsible AI adoption. Alan Lim, Director and Head, Digital and Infrastructure, AI Office, Monetary Authority of Singapore, argued that governance should not be viewed as an obstacle to innovation. Instead, clear guardrails provide institutions with the confidence to innovate more rapidly. He noted that while many governance disciplines, including model risk management and data governance, already existed before Gen AI, new challenges have emerged because large language models produce non-deterministic outputs. Unlike traditional rules-based systems, identical prompts may generate different responses, making consistency, validation and explainability significantly more complex within highly regulated financial environments. Balaji Rajagopalan, Chief Technology Officer, State Bank of India Alan Lim, Director and Head, Digital and Infrastructure, AI Office, Monetary Authority of Singapore A similar balance between innovation and prudence emerged from Japan. Jutaro Kaneko, Deputy Commissioner for International Affairs, Financial Services Agency, Japan, explained that the regulator has deliberately refrained from introducing AI-specific financial regulation at this stage, preferring continued dialogue with industry while identifying emerging risks that may require future intervention. At the same time, the agency has sought to encourage adoption by supporting common AI capabilities for regional banks, reflecting the view that governance should enable innovation rather than discourage it. From Indonesia, Muhammad Zikri, Director of Data Innovation and Digitalisation Department, Bank of Indonesia, described a framework centred on proportional risk management, lifecycle governance, accountability and human oversight. He argued that trustworthy AI depends fundamentally on trustworthy data, observing that explainability, fairness and model reliability cannot be achieved without disciplined data governance throughout the AI lifecycle. His emphasis reflected a broader regulatory trend in which AI governance increasingly begins with data governance rather than algorithms themselves. Jutaro Kaneko, Deputy Commissioner for International Affairs, Financial Services Agency, Japan Muhammad Zikri, Director of Data Innovation and Digitalisation Department, Bank of Indonesia Taken together, these perspectives suggest that enterprise-wide digital trust cannot be achieved by strengthening cybersecurity alone. Instead, it requires institutions to integrate AI governance, data governance, operational resilience, cyber risk management and executive accountability into a unified operating model. As AI becomes embedded across banking, governance increasingly shifts from being a compliance function to becoming an enterprise capability that determines whether institutions can deploy intelligent technologies safely, responsibly and at scale. Trustworthy AI as the next competitive advantage For much of the past two decades, banks competed primarily on digital capability. Institutions invested heavily in mobile banking, cloud infrastructure, application programming interfaces (APIs), automation and data platforms to improve customer experience and operational efficiency. As AI becomes embedded across virtually every banking function, however, competitive differentiation is beginning to shift. The question is no longer which institution deploys the most AI, but which can demonstrate that its AI remains secure, explainable, resilient and trustworthy throughout its lifecycle. This represents a significant change in the industry’s strategic priorities. During the first wave of digital transformation, technology investment was largely measured through adoption rates, speed of deployment and customer convenience. AI introduces an additional dimension. Institutions must now demonstrate that automated decisions remain consistent with regulatory expectations, organisational risk appetite and customer interests even as models evolve, learn and interact with increasingly autonomous systems. Trust therefore becomes an operational capability rather than simply a customer perception. This distinction will become increasingly important as AI moves beyond productivity tools into decision-making processes. The early phase of AI adoption has focused largely on copilots, code generation, customer service assistants and workflow automation. These applications generally operate with relatively low levels of autonomy and retain significant human oversight. The next phase is expected to involve AI agents capable of initiating transactions, coordinating multiple business processes and interacting directly with customers and external systems. This progression substantially increases both the value and the risk associated with AI deployment. Duran observed that banks should therefore avoid becoming overly focused on predicting a single technological destination. Instead, they should build organisational capabilities that allow them to adapt as AI continues to evolve. Whether future banking involves AI agents acting on behalf of customers, autonomous payment initiation or entirely new forms of customer interaction remains uncertain. What is more predictable is that institutions with stronger governance, better data quality and more adaptable operating models will be better positioned to respond as these developments materialise. Rajagopalan similarly argued that AI investments should continue to be evaluated through measurable business outcomes rather than technological novelty. For banks, productivity gains, faster turnaround times, improved customer experiences, stronger fraud detection and better resource utilisation remain the primary indicators of success. AI should therefore be deployed where it demonstrably improves business performance rather than because it represents the latest technological trend. This emphasis on business value reflects an important shift away from technology-led transformation towards outcome-led transformation. Trust extends beyond AI models themselves to the quality of the data supporting them. Data governance is therefore the foundation of responsible AI. This is particularly significant because many AI failures originate not from model architecture but from incomplete, biased or poorly governed data. Financial institutions have long invested in data quality to support regulatory reporting and risk management. AI raises the stakes further because unreliable data can directly affect automated recommendations, customer interactions and operational decisions. Ironically, institutions may find that AI itself becomes one of the least differentiated aspects of their operating model. Foundation models are becoming increasingly accessible through cloud platforms and commercial software providers. What remains difficult to replicate is the institutional capability to govern those models consistently across thousands of employees, business processes and customer interactions. Competitive advantage may therefore shift away from algorithms themselves towards organisational discipline. Regulators increasingly share this perspective. Lim noted that many of the governance disciplines required for Gen AI, including model risk management, data governance and operational controls, already existed before the arrival of large language models. Rather than replacing these disciplines, AI amplifies their importance. Gen AI introduces new characteristics such as non-deterministic outputs, but institutions that have established mature governance foundations are generally better positioned to manage these additional risks. Zikri’s emphasis that “trusted AI requires trusted data” reinforces this broader principle. Explainability, fairness and reliability cannot be achieved if institutions cannot demonstrate the provenance, integrity and governance of the data underpinning AI systems. As banks deploy increasingly sophisticated models, data governance is therefore becoming inseparable from AI governance itself. Another recurring theme was the continued importance of human judgement. Despite rapid advances in AI capability, neither regulators nor industry practitioners suggested that human oversight should disappear from banking. Instead, the discussion focused on identifying where human intervention remains essential and where greater automation may become appropriate. This represents a more nuanced position than the often-polarised debate surrounding AI replacing human decision-makers. Kaneko raised an important consideration in this context by questioning how effective human oversight remains when people themselves are susceptible to automation bias and cognitive bias. If users naturally place excessive confidence in AI-generated recommendations, simply requiring a human to approve an AI decision may not provide the safeguard many institutions assume it does. This observation shifts attention from the presence of humans in governance processes towards the quality and independence of their judgement. Similarly, Khraishi suggested that human review is likely to remain necessary for many higher-risk banking activities, including credit decision-making in jurisdictions where regulatory expectations require meaningful human involvement. At the same time, lower-risk internal applications are increasingly likely to become fully automated as institutions gain greater confidence in AI reliability and governance. The issue therefore is not whether humans remain involved, but how organisations determine the appropriate balance between automation and oversight across different use cases. This balance increasingly influences customer confidence as well. Customers rarely evaluate AI models directly. Instead, they judge the quality of financial institutions through the consistency, fairness and reliability of the services they receive. A highly accurate model that occasionally produces unexplained or inconsistent outcomes may ultimately undermine confidence more than a slightly less sophisticated system operating within well-understood governance boundaries. Trust therefore becomes observable through predictable customer outcomes rather than technological complexity. Looking ahead, this emphasis on trust is likely to influence investment priorities across the banking industry. While institutions will continue investing in Gen AI, agentic AI and intelligent automation, they are also likely to devote increasing resources to model validation, continuous assurance, behavioural monitoring, identity protection, cyber resilience and quantum-resistant cryptography. These investments may not always produce visible customer features, but they are becoming essential infrastructure for maintaining confidence in increasingly autonomous financial systems. Trustworthy AI may become a competitive capability rather than merely a regulatory requirement. Institutions that can demonstrate disciplined governance, transparent decision-making and resilient AI operations are likely to enjoy greater confidence from regulators, customers and counterparties alike. As AI becomes ubiquitous across financial services, trust may prove harder to replicate than the technology itself, making it one of the industry’s most enduring sources of competitive advantage. Securing confidence in an autonomous financial system The financial industry has experienced several waves of technological transformation over the past three decades, from internet banking and mobile payments to cloud computing and open banking. Each has introduced new efficiencies while exposing new vulnerabilities. AI differs in one important respect: it is simultaneously changing how financial institutions operate, how customers interact with them and how attackers seek to exploit them. The same technology that enables greater productivity also lowers the barriers to increasingly sophisticated cybercrime, making trust the central strategic challenge of the next phase of banking. This convergence requires a broader conception of resilience than the industry has traditionally adopted. Historically, cybersecurity focused on protecting networks, applications and infrastructure from external attack. Operational resilience expanded that scope to include business continuity, third-party risk and critical operations. AI now adds another layer, requiring institutions to govern intelligent systems whose behaviour may evolve over time, interact autonomously with other systems and influence decisions across virtually every business function. As a result, digital trust is no longer the responsibility of a single technology or security function but an enterprise-wide capability spanning governance, risk management, technology, operations and leadership. Whether examining AI-enabled fraud, enterprise governance or board oversight, participants repeatedly returned to the need for integration rather than specialisation. Cybersecurity cannot operate independently of AI governance. AI governance cannot be separated from data governance. Operational resilience cannot be maintained without understanding how autonomous systems influence critical business processes. These disciplines increasingly reinforce one another, requiring institutions to develop operating models capable of managing technology as an interconnected ecosystem rather than as a collection of individual projects. The role of leadership is also changing. Boards are no longer expected merely to approve technology investments; they must increasingly understand how AI affects institutional risk, customer trust and strategic resilience. Similarly, chief information security officers are evolving from technical specialists into enterprise risk leaders responsible for communicating cyber risk in business terms, prioritising investments and demonstrating how security enables sustainable innovation. Ng argued that cybersecurity should be viewed not simply as a cost but as a means of preserving a bank’s licence to operate, with stakeholder engagement and measurable delivery being essential to securing long-term organisational support. Regulators, meanwhile, appear to be converging around broadly consistent principles despite differences in national implementation. Across Singapore, Japan and Indonesia, the emphasis was not on restricting AI adoption but on ensuring that innovation remains proportionate to risk, supported by robust governance and subject to meaningful accountability. Despite differences in regulatory philosophy, the three authorities converged on several common principles. None advocated slowing AI adoption. Instead, each emphasised proportional governance, strong data management, human accountability and continuous oversight as the foundations for responsible deployment. While regulatory frameworks will undoubtedly continue to evolve, the discussions suggested that many of the underlying expectations, sound data governance, model validation, transparency, human accountability and operational resilience, are already becoming established supervisory norms rather than emerging concepts. Looking ahead, the competitive landscape is also likely to evolve. AI capabilities themselves are becoming increasingly accessible through foundation models, cloud platforms and commercial software. Over time, many technical capabilities may become widely available across the industry, reducing their ability to differentiate one institution from another. What is likely to prove more difficult to replicate is the organisational capability to deploy AI consistently, securely and responsibly at scale. Institutions that can demonstrate disciplined governance, reliable operations and sustained customer confidence may therefore enjoy advantages that are considerably more durable than early technological adoption alone. The next generation of banking technology investment is unlikely to be judged by how much AI institutions deploy, but by how confidently they can demonstrate that AI remains secure, explainable and resilient under real operating conditions. Banks will continue expanding AI across customer engagement, risk management, software engineering and operational automation, but these initiatives will increasingly be accompanied by investment in continuous assurance, behavioural analytics, identity protection, model monitoring, supply-chain security and quantum-resistant cryptography. Rather than viewing these as compliance costs, institutions may increasingly regard them as foundational infrastructure supporting the safe deployment of intelligent financial services. Every major technology transformation in banking has eventually become mainstream. ATMs, internet banking, mobile banking, cloud computing and APIs all followed that trajectory. AI is unlikely to be different. Models will become more powerful, less expensive and increasingly accessible to every institution. What will remain scarce is trust. Customers, regulators and counterparties will continue to judge financial institutions not by the sophistication of their algorithms but by the consistency, transparency and resilience of the decisions those algorithms produce. In that environment, digital trust becomes more than a security objective or regulatory requirement. It becomes an institutional capability that enables innovation at scale, making it one of the defining competitive advantages of banking in the AI economy.

title: Maybank Group Sustainability Week 2026 advances net zero ambitions through capacity building and collective action | Maybank
body: In its third year, MGSW 2026 recognised over 1000 certified sustainability practitioners & continues to inspire greater net zero action across the Group Maybank recently organised the Maybank Group Sustainability Week (MGSW) 2026, a three-day sustainability-focused programme held from 21 to 23 September 2026 at Menara Merdeka Maybank. Under the theme “Net Zero. From Commitment to Action”, MGSW 2026 focuses on advancing Maybank’s net zero journey through capacity building, deepening sustainability awareness and strengthening capabilities, in line with the Group’s ROAR30 sustainability ambitions. MGSW 2026 saw Maybankers across the Group participate in two key events; ‘Net Zero Week’, which featured a series of learning, engagement and experiential activities, and the ‘Maybank Sustainability Practitioner Certification (MSPC) Open Day’ and ‘Grand Conferment Ceremony’, which celebrated over 1,000 certified sustainability practitioners and inspiring Maybankers to advance in their sustainability journey. The event saw the attendance of Dato' Sri Khairussaleh Ramli, President & Group CEO Maybank, Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Group Chief Sustainability Officer Maybank, Board of Directors and Group EXCO members of Maybank, Dato’ Ir. Ts. (Dr.) Izwan Hasli Mohd Ibrahim, CEO PNB Merdeka Ventures, Muazzam Mohamad, Head of Corporate Sustainability & Stewardship PNB, Leo Pui Yong, Chief Sustainability Officer Tenaga Nasional Berhad and Edey Suresh Kumar Manikam, Board Director at Large UN Global Compact Network Malaysia, Brunei & Cambodia (UNGCMBC). Dato' Sri Khairussaleh Ramli said “As we advance in our sustainability journey, MGSW 2026 reflects our continued focus on enabling our people to support our customers' transition journeys to net zero through stronger knowledge and mindsets. Ultimately, our commitment to capacity building will in turn help our customers transition responsibly and sustainably, strengthen our communities and drive meaningful sustainability impact.” A key highlight of MGSW 2026 was the MSPC Grand Conferment Ceremony, which honoured 36 MSPC Level 3 Red Belt graduates from across the Group for their achievements and continued commitment in sustainability. Developed in partnership with UNGCMBC, the MSPC programme was introduced in 2023 with the vision of building a future-ready sustainability workforce. Through its four-tier certification pathway comprising Level 1 White, Level 2 Green, Level 3 Red and Level 4 Black Belt levels, the programme combines sustainability knowledge with practical application to equip Maybankers with the capabilities needed to drive sustainability initiatives across the organisation. Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli, President & Group CEO Maybank (Center in blue batik), Dato’ Ir. Ts. (Dr.) Izwan Hasli Mohd Ibrahim, CEO PNB Merdeka Ventures (In red tie) and Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Group Chief Sustainability Officer Maybank (In black blazer with glasses) posing with the MSPC Level 1 White Belt recipients at the MSPC Grand Conferment ceremony during the MGSW 2026. As the entry level of the MSPC programme, the certification equips Maybankers with the foundational knowledge and capabilities needed to drive sustainability initiatives across the Group. A key highlight of the MSPC ceremony was the recognition of the 36 MSPC Level 3 Red Belt graduates from across the Group. Since its inception, MSPC has grown into a network of sustainability practitioners across the Group, spanning more than 60 cohorts and expands beyond Malaysia to Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines and Cambodia. To date, the programme has enrolled more than 2,300 participants and certified 1,755 practitioners. Maybankers came together throughout the three-day MGSW 2026 to learn, engage and take action on sustainability through a diverse range of interactive workshops, experiential activities, sharing sessions and challenges, reflecting the Group’s commitment to advancing its net zero journey under the theme “Net Zero. From Commitment to Action.” As a pioneering initiative and a first of its kind in the industry, MSPC is a sustainability capability programme built on a structured belting system, demonstrating how a financial institution can systematically empower its people with the knowledge, skills and credibility needed to deliver sustainable impact. Maybankers participated in a weaving activity at the Women Eco Weavers booth by Maybank Foundation during the MGSW 2026, transforming used fabric into handcrafted products while promoting how traditional craftsmanship can support waste reduction and sustainable livelihood. “The MSPC ceremony marks another significant milestone in our journey towards becoming the sustainability leader in ASEAN as it is ultimately a celebration of our people. It recognises Maybankers who have committed themselves to developing the knowledge and skills needed to advance our sustainability ambitions. It also reflects how far we have progressed, from building awareness and advocacy to strengthening action and accountability across the Group.” said Dato' Sri Khairussaleh Ramli. MGSW 2026 also saw the launch of the ‘Plastic Bottle Recycling’ initiative between Maybank, PNB and PNB Merdeka Ventures to encourage greater environmental responsibility among occupants of Menara Merdeka Maybank. The initiative was launched by Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli, Dato’ Izwan Hasli and Muazzam Mohamad through a symbolic recycling activity. As part of the initiative, dedicated plastic bottle recycling bins will be deployed across Menara Merdeka Maybank to encourage proper waste segregation and foster a greener, more environmentally conscious community. Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli, President & Group CEO of Maybank, together with Muazzam Mohamad and Dato’ Ir. Ts. (Dr.) Izwan Hasli Mohd Ibrahim, officiates the launch of the Plastic Bottle Recycling initiative through a symbolic recycling activity during MGSW 2026. The programme featured a diverse range of learning, engagement, and experiential activities through initiatives such as Net Zero Zone, MSPC Experience Zone, Sustainability Marketplace, Upcycling Activities, Sustainability Tree, the Relationship Manager’s Net Zero Challenge, and #MaybankCares Points. Maybankers participated in the creation of reusable tote bags made from used clothing at the ‘Upcycling booth’ during the MGSW 2026, highlighting the importance of waste reduction, resource circularity and sustainable everyday practices. A series of expert-led discussions, workshops and sharing sessions covered topics such as “Talk to Traction: Solving the Net Zero Equation Across Sustainability, Business and Law.”, “From Energy Optimisation to Net Zero”, Menara Merdeka Maybank Green Building Sharing Session and Social Impact Partners’ Day. Concurrently, the Etiqa Sustainability Day was also held in conjunction with MGSW 2026, where they hosted workshops, sharing sessions and a Sustainability Bazaar at Dataran Maybank. Maybankers participated in expert-led discussions, workshops and knowledge-sharing sessions during Maybank Group Sustainability Week (MGSW) 2026, which covered topics ranging from net zero transition and energy optimisation to sustainable building practices and social impact, aimed at strengthening sustainability knowledge and action across the Group. Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin said “MGSW demonstrates the growing momentum of sustainability within Maybank. The enthusiasm and participation shown by Maybankers throughout the week reinforces our belief that continued progress is driven by a shared sense of purpose and responsibility. We are encouraged by this momentum and are confident it will continue to shape the way sustainability is embraced across the Group.” Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Group Chief Sustainability Officer Maybank (Center in Black blazer) sharing a light moment with participants of the Sustainable Manager Portfolio Challenge during the MGSW 2026. The interactive competition simulated real-world portfolio management scenarios, challenging participants to balance profitability, business growth and sustainability considerations in their decision-making. As part of its commitment in transitioning towards a low-carbon economy, Maybank has achieved a cumulative 58.9% reduction in operational carbon emissions since 2021, marking significant progress towards its target of a 61% reduction by 2026. The achievement reflects the Group’s continued efforts to reduce its environmental footprint while advancing its long-term ambitions of achieving carbon neutrality by 2030 and net zero emissions by 2050.

title: Best Study Loans in Malaysia: PTPTN vs Banks
body: What Are Your Study Loan Options in Malaysia? When it comes to funding your higher education, you generally have four paths to choose from. It is always wise to look at them in this specific order: 1. The "Bank of Mom and Dad" (Family Support) If your parents or family members have an education fund set aside for you, this is your best option. It is interest-free, comes with zero debt stress, and requires no complicated paperwork. 2. Scholarships and Government Grants Scholarships do not require monetary repayment. However, they are highly competitive and often come with "bonding periods," requiring you to work for the sponsoring company or government body for a set number of years after graduating. 3. PTPTN Study Loans The default choice for the majority of Malaysian students. It is highly accessible, easy to apply for, and charges an incredibly low flat administrative rate (Kos Upah). 4. Commercial Bank Education Loans Banks like Maybank, Bank Rakyat, and Affin Bank offer dedicated education financing. While they can cover higher tuition fees (especially for expensive courses like medicine or overseas pilot programs), they come with much higher interest rates and stricter eligibility criteria. PTPTN vs. Bank Education Loans: How Do They Compare? To help you visualise the difference, here is a quick comparison of what you can expect: (Please verify the latest rates and terms on the official bank or PTPTN websites before applying.) Can You Combine PTPTN with a Scholarship? This is a very common question. The short answer is: it depends on the type of scholarship. If your university offers a partial tuition fee waiver or a merit discount directly on your semester fees, you are usually still eligible to apply for PTPTN to cover the remaining balance or your cost of living. This helps ease your overall financial burden. However, if you have secured a full, third-party sponsorship (from corporate giants like Yayasan Petronas, JPA, or Sime Darby), their terms and conditions will almost certainly prohibit you from taking a PTPTN loan simultaneously. Always check with your university’s student affairs department before signing any agreements. The Million-Ringgit Question: Should You Pay Off PTPTN Early? A PTPTN loan charges a flat administrative rate of 1% per annum. In the world of finance, this is virtually free money. A 1% flat rate translates to a very low effective interest rate (roughly 1.8% to 1.9%). Imagine you have a RM50,000 PTPTN loan with a 15-year repayment period. Your minimum monthly repayment is roughly RM319.44. If you have extra cash on hand after graduating, you have two choices: - Option 1: Pay off the loan as slowly as possible and put your extra cash into high-yield savings accounts, digital banks (which offer up to 3% to 4% p.a.), or low-risk investments like ASB or EPF (which historical data shows yield 4.5% to 6% p.a.). - Option 2: Pay off the loan quickly in 5 to 10 years to live a debt-free life. Scientifically speaking, Option 1 makes more financial sense. Because the interest rate of PTPTN (1%) is significantly lower than the dividend rates of ASB or digital banks, your money grows faster in an investment account than the debt accumulates. However, Option 2 gives you peace of mind and improves your Debt Service Ratio (DSR). This makes it much easier to apply for home loans and car loans later in life. The Real Consequences of Ignoring Your PTPTN Repayments During our interviews with university graduates, we noticed a worrying trend: many do not take PTPTN repayment seriously. Some assume that because they are "government loans," they can simply be ignored. This is a massive mistake. If you fail to repay your PTPTN loan, you will face severe long-term financial consequences. Your CCRIS Score Will Be Ruined PTPTN is linked directly to the Central Credit Reference Information System (CCRIS) managed by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM). If you default on your payments, your CCRIS report will show black marks. When you apply for a credit card, a car loan for your first Axia, or a home loan, banks will pull your CCRIS report. If they see unpaid PTPTN dues, your application will be instantly rejected. Legal Action and Debt Collectors PTPTN has the right to take legal action against you. You will be issued letters of demand, and in worst-case scenarios, your bank accounts or salary could be subject to garnishment. Travel Bans (An Ongoing Possibility) While the blanket immigration travel ban was suspended a few years ago to ease the burden on young graduates, PTPTN reserves the right to re-enact travel restrictions for chronic defaulters. Don't risk getting stopped at KLIA on your way to a holiday or an overseas work trip. FAQs About PTPTN Q: Can I get my PTPTN loan waived if I graduate with First Class Honours? A: Yes! PTPTN still offers a loan-to-scholarship conversion (exemption from repayment) for students who graduate with First Class Honours. However, this is subject to specific criteria, such as graduating within the prospective time frame and applying within 12 months of your graduation date. Q: Can I use my EPF savings to pay off my PTPTN loan? A: Yes, you can. Under the revised EPF structure, you can make withdrawals from your Akaun Sejahtera (Account 2) to pay off your own PTPTN loan or even your children's PTPTN loans. This is a great way to settle your debt without affecting your monthly cash flow. Q: Is there a grace period before I have to start paying back? A: Yes. PTPTN gives you a 12-month grace period after you complete your studies before you are required to start making repayments. This timeline gives you enough buffer to secure a stable job first. Q: How do I easily manage and track my PTPTN repayments? A: You can download the official MyPTPTN app on your smartphone. It allows you to check your outstanding balance, make direct payments via FPX, set up direct debits, and even open or top up your SSPN savings accounts. Summary: The TL;DR on PTPTN - Unbeatable Interest Rates: At a 1% flat rate, PTPTN is still the cheapest and most accessible study loan in Malaysia. - CCRIS is Real: Failing to pay back your PTPTN loan will ruin your credit score, making it impossible to buy a car or a home in the future. - Repayment is Flexible: You can use your EPF Akaun Sejahtera to make lump-sum payments. - Strive for the Best: Aiming for a First Class Honours degree can completely wipe out your debt. Conclusion Is PTPTN still the best study loan for Malaysian students? Yes, absolutely. No commercial bank in Malaysia can match its 1% administrative fee, nor do they offer loan waivers for high-achieving students. Just remember: PTPTN is a revolving fund. When you pay back your loan, you are directly funding the education of the next generation of Malaysian students. Take charge of your finances, make your repayments on time, and build a strong financial foundation for your adult life. Compare your loan and savings options with Loanstreet’s financial calculators to see how you can best manage your money today. Taking proactive steps now will set you up for a much brighter financial future.

title: Building on a legacy of Art and Community: Maybank returns for the third edition of CASB 2026 | Maybank
body: Since inception, CASB has attracted over 10,000 visitors and generated more than RM460,000 for artisans and cultural practitioners, championing cultural expression and economic empowerment Celebrating the people at the heart of CASB 2026 - Participating artisans proudly receive their Certificates of Appreciation in recognition of their talent, dedication and contribution to Malaysia’s creative and cultural landscape. Joining them are (L-R middle row, standing): Mr. Surin Segar A/L Gnanasegaram, Head, Group Tax Maybank & Chief Financial Officer of Maybank Foundation (in a blue, short-sleeve batik shirt); Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer (in a blue, long-sleeve batik shirt); Datin Paduka Marina Mahathir, member of Board of Trustees, Maybank Foundation (in purple kebaya); Puan Josefine Midong anak Jubin of Tanoti from the Maybank Women Eco-Weavers (MWEW) programme (in black and floral kebaya); Puan Putri Shahda Azza Binti Megat Burhainuddin, Deputy Director, Policy and Research Division (Policy), Jabatan Kebudayaan dan Kesenian Negara (JKKN) (in pink kurung batik); Dr. Yasmin Rasyid, General Manager, Sustainability, Sime Darby Property (in a black and floral ensemble) & Datuk R. Karunakaran, member of Board of Trustees, Maybank Foundation (in a purple batik shirt). Maybank Foundation, the social impact arm of Maybank Group, celebrates the return of the Cultural Art Showcase and Bazaar (CASB) 2026, reaffirming its continued commitment to preserving Malaysia’s rich cultural heritage and creating meaningful opportunities for local artisans and cultural practitioners. Now in its third edition, CASB 2026 is being held from 20 August to 20 September 2026 at KLGCC Mall, Kuala Lumpur, bringing together artisans, cultural practitioners, performers and creative communities in a month-long celebration of Malaysia’s diverse cultural identity. The showcase is held in conjunction with the nation’s Hari Kebangsaan and Hari Malaysia celebrations. The official the launch of CASB 2026 - Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer and Dr. Yasmin Rasyid, General Manager, Sustainability, Sime Darby Property took centre stage, officiating the month-long celebration of Malaysia’s rich cultural heritage and creative talent at the Cultural Art Showcase and Bazaar (CASB) 2026. They are joined by (from L-R): En. Ahmad Hilmi Hashim, Head of Technical Management and Governance, Group Sustainability Maybank (in brown batik shirt); Datin Paduka Marina Mahathir; member of Board of Trustees, Maybank Foundation; Mr. Surin Segar A/L Gnanasegaram, Head, Group Tax Maybank and Chief Financial Officer of Maybank Foundation; Puan Putri Shahda Azza Binti Megat Burhainuddin, Deputy Director, Policy and Research Division (Policy), Jabatan Kebudayaan dan Kesenian Negara (JKKN); Fadzlin Ariffin, Head of Community Empowerment, Maybank Foundation (in light blue kebaya batik); Datuk R. Karunakaran, member of Board of Trustees, Maybank Foundation & Rizqan Helmi Mohd Ariff, Head, Asset Management, Sime Darby Property (in a dark purple batik shirt). Visitors to CASB 2026 can experience cultural performances featuring traditional music, dance, theatre and contemporary interpretations of Malaysia’s diverse cultural heritage, Artisanal workshops led by participating practitioners, Artisan showcases and booths featuring a diverse range of Malaysian craftsmanship, including weaving, beading, batik, wau-making, indigenous art and other traditional crafts and Local F&B offerings, showcasing regional flavours that provide a platform for homegrown culinary talents. The 2026 programme features cultural groups such as Sanggar Seni Malaysia, Nyala Dance Theatre, Persatuan Kompang Cahaya Murni, Iron Gang Puppet Theatre, KRATE Creative Space and Sri Dasmesh Pipe Band. It also features two rotating groups of artisans and artisanal brands throughout the showcase, allowing more creative entrepreneurs to participate while refreshing the visitor experience, exposure and market access across the month. The launch came alive with a vibrant Borneo-fusion performance by Nyala Dance Theatre, inspired by the Ngajat of Sarawak and Sumazau of Sabah. Bringing movement, rhythm and tradition to the stage. The performance set the tone for CASB 2026, a lively celebration of the diverse cultural expressions that makes Malaysia unique. The Artisan Appreciation Ceremony, which marks the halfway point of the showcase was graced by Datin Paduka Marina Mahathir and Datuk Karunakaran A/L Ramasamy, Members of the Maybank Foundation Board of Trustees; Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer; Dr Yasmin Binti Rasyid, General Manager, Sustainability, Sime Darby Property; Puan Putri Shahda Azza Binti Megat Burhainuddin, Deputy Director, Policy and Research Division (Policy), Jabatan Kebudayaan dan Kesenian Negara (JKKN) and Puan Anita Ahmad, CEO, Yayasan MySDG. From celebration to participation - Dr. Yasmin Rasyid, General Manager, Sustainability, Sime Darby Property (in white dress) gets hands-on with traditional weaving, guided by Puan Josefine Midong anak Jubin of Tanoti from the Maybank Women Eco-Weavers (MWEW) programme, one of the 40 artisans featured at CASB 2026. Against a vibrant backdrop of woven textiles, the moment reflects CASB’s role in bringing heritage closer to the community while creating meaningful platforms for artisans to share their knowledge and craft. Speaking at the Artisan Appreciation Ceremony, Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer, said, “CASB reflects what it means to impact society positively by creating opportunities for communities, celebrating our shared heritage and bringing people together through culture and creativity. Initiatives such as CASB demonstrate how cultural programmes can create impact beyond the arts by supporting livelihoods, strengthening community connections and providing greater visibility for the people who keep Malaysia’s traditions alive.” Connecting Artisans, Partners and Community - Engaging with the people at the heart of CASB 2026, Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer (in a blue, long-sleeve batik shirt), Datuk Karunakaran A/L Ramasamy, member of Board of Trustees, Maybank Foundation (in a purple batik shirt), along with Fadzlin Ariffin, Head of Community Empowerment, Maybank Foundation (in light blue kebaya batik), engaging with Puan Josefine Midong anak Jubin, a fellow weaver from the Maybank Women Eco-Weavers (MWEW) programme, showcasing her artisanal products from Tanoti. Also pictured is Miss Elvina, Tanoti’s programme coordinator (in black shirt, with glasses). The exchange reflects the spirit of CASB, connecting artisans, partners and audiences to create greater visibility and opportunities for Malaysia’s creative communities. “More importantly, CASB represents something much bigger than a cultural showcase or bazaar. It is aligned with Maybank Group’s ROAR30 aspiration, particularly our commitment to Impacting Society Positively (ISP), which seeks to ensure that Maybank’s growth translates into meaningful and lasting benefits for the communities we serve. Under this pillar alone, the Group has mobilised more than RM30 million towards Social Empowerment initiatives and positively impacted over 466,000 individuals. As part of this journey, Maybank remains firmly on track towards its aspiration of empowering three million lives by 2030. CASB is part of this broader commitment, demonstrating how arts and culture can inspire learning, strengthen community bonds and create opportunities for greater social inclusion, and contribute meaningfully to this shared goal,” added Datuk Shahril. The showcase continues to be supported through Maybank Foundation’s partnership with Kakiseni, while Maybank MAE serves as the digital payment platform for the initiative. CASB 2026 is also made possible through collaboration with Sime Darby Property as the strategic venue partner, which hosts the showcase at KLGCC Mall, its third wholly-owned mall. Building on the momentum of its first two editions, CASB has welcomed more than 10,000 visitors and generated over RM460,000 in cumulative income for featured artisans and cultural practitioners since its inception in 2024. This year, CASB continues to strengthen its role as a platform for cultural expression and economic empowerment, providing artisans with opportunities to reach new audiences, showcase their craft and connect with potential customers. Turning skills into opportunities - En. Azmi bin Taha, representing the seven participants from the Reach Independence & Sustainable Entrepreneurship (R.I.S.E.) programme, received a Certificate of Appreciation from Datuk Shahril Azuar Jimin, Maybank Group Chief Sustainability Officer witnessed by Fadzlin Ariffin, Head of Community Empowerment, Maybank Foundation. The recognition underscores CASB’s commitment to creating inclusive platforms where talent from various skillsets can be showcased, valued and translated into meaningful economic opportunities. As a key programme under the Balai Seni Art Series (BSAS), CASB is part of Maybank Foundation’s longstanding commitment to making arts and culture more accessible to communities, creating platforms for artists and cultural practitioners to thrive. Since the inception of BSAS in 1988, the programme has supported over 9,300 artists and beneficiaries through exhibitions and cultural initiatives. CASB builds on this legacy by bringing art, culture and community directly into spaces where people live, work and gather. The continued growth of CASB reflects Maybank Foundation’s broader commitment to catalysing positive and sustainable change, particularly through its three key pillars of Community Empowerment, Empowering Education and Environmental Diversity. By creating platforms for cultural participation and economic opportunity. The public is welcomed to visit CASB 2026 at KLGCC Mall, Level 1, Main Atrium, Kuala Lumpur till 20 September 2026. Showcases and activities will commence from 10.00am – 10.00pm daily. Visit www.maybankfoundation.com for more information on CASB 2026.

title: Maybank Commits RM10 Billion to Technology and Growth Under ROAR30
body: Maybank is committing RM10 billion in investment through 2030 as it expands its ROAR30 strategy across technology, regional banking, payments, wealth management and sustainability. The banking group plans to spend RM1.5 billion on technology during FY2026 alone. Its investment programme will cover core system modernisation, artificial intelligence, cloud adoption, resilience improvements and stronger risk and compliance capabilities. Maybank expects those investments to help it increase productivity while providing more personalised services across its regional operations. The programme comes as the group reported RM5.17 billion in net profit for the first half of FY2026. Technology Becomes Central to Maybank ROAR30 Maybank is positioning technology as an important enabler of its next phase of regional growth. The group intends to modernise core banking infrastructure while expanding the use of AI and cloud technologies. It is also investing in systems designed to improve operational resilience and strengthen compliance capabilities. President and Group CEO Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli said technology was already helping Maybank deepen customer engagement, scale its businesses and improve productivity. The ROAR30 strategy will place greater emphasis on businesses where Maybank believes it can establish or extend regional leadership. These include Islamic finance, wealth management, transaction banking, payments, corporate and investment banking, and SMEs. Wealth and Investment Banking Fees Rise Several of Maybank’s targeted growth areas recorded stronger performance during the first half of FY2026. Wealth fee income increased 49.6% year-on-year to RM925.4 million. Corporate and investment banking fee income rose 15.6% to RM1.51 billion. Cross-border payments volume increased 15.8% to RM465.2 billion. Maybank also continued expanding its Islamic financial services business. Islamic corporate and investment banking income increased 3.9% year-on-year to RM896.8 million. Takaful net written contribution rose 10.2% to RM1.72 billion. The figures support Maybank’s strategy of increasing revenue from fee-based and regional businesses alongside traditional lending. Maybank Declares 31 Sen Interim Dividend Shareholders will also receive a higher first interim dividend following Maybank’s resilient first-half performance. The board declared 31 sen per share, compared with 30 sen per share for the first half of FY2025. Five sen per share will be electable under Maybank’s Dividend Reinvestment Plan. The dividend represents an estimated total payout of RM3.75 billion. That amount is equivalent to approximately 72.5% of Maybank’s first-half net profit. The payout highlights the group’s attempt to balance shareholder returns with continued investment in technology, growth and balance-sheet resilience. Maybank maintained a Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 14.92% as of June 2026. Its total capital ratio stood at 18.68%. Sustainable Finance Reaches RM31.81 Billion Sustainability remains another major component of Maybank’s longer-term strategy. The group mobilised RM31.81 billion in sustainable finance as of June 2026. It also mobilised RM12.86 billion in social finance and RM30.96 million through social empowerment initiatives during the same period. Maybank said these programmes benefited more than 268,000 people. More than 238,000 people were reached through financial inclusion initiatives, while approximately 30,000 participated in financial literacy programmes. Maybank has refreshed its long-term sustainable finance ambition to RM300 billion by 2030. It is also targeting RM24 billion in annual social finance, with programmes intended to economically empower three million people. Maybank Cuts Operational Carbon Emissions The group reported a 58.9% reduction in carbon emissions against its baseline. That places Maybank close to its 2026 target of a 61% reduction. Its longer-term goals include achieving carbon neutrality by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050. Maybank also reported continued progress across six priority sectors within its financed emissions portfolio. Physical emissions intensity has declined 23% in power, 13% in palm oil and 10% in commercial real estate since the baseline year. Automotive emissions intensity declined 8%. Steel and aluminium remained below their respective emissions glidepaths. Maybank said those improvements reflected portfolio management, client engagement and increased exposure to lower-emitting assets. ROAR30 Targets Regional Leadership Maybank Chairman Tan Sri Dato’ Sri Ir. Zamzamzairani Mohd Isa said the group’s capital and liquidity positions provide a strong foundation for navigating changing market conditions. He also emphasised the group’s commitment to responsible growth, shareholder value and sustainability. Khairussaleh said Maybank would continue sharpening its focus on businesses where it can lead while strengthening capabilities across the region. The strategy combines several priorities that traditionally compete for capital. Maybank intends to continue paying meaningful shareholder dividends while investing heavily in technology and pursuing regional growth. At the same time, the group is increasing sustainable finance commitments and working towards progressively tighter emissions targets. Its RM10 billion investment programme therefore represents more than a technology upgrade. It forms part of a broader attempt to position Maybank for the next phase of Southeast Asian banking, where digital services, regional scale, fee income and sustainability are becoming increasingly important sources of competitive advantage.

title: Maybank dan UMSKAL perkasa generasi pelajar Labuan ke arah masa depan pendidikan yang cemerlang
body: Nor Rashidi (tengah), Profesor Dr. Shamsul Bahari (dua kanan), Imbran (kiri) dan Nur Iman (kanan) bergambar kenangan bersama pelajar yang menjayakan Program Maybank Global CR Day 2026: “Cahaya Future Ready” LABUAN: Maybank International Labuan Branch dengan kerjasama Bahagian Hal Ehwal Pelajar UMSKAL telah menganjurkan Program Maybank Global CR Day 2026 yang diadakan di Dewan Theatrette, Universiti Malaysia Sabah Kampus Antarabangsa Labuan (UMSKAL) pada Sabtu. Program yang berlangsung sehari itu bertujuan memberi pendedahan serta motivasi kepada pelajar sekolah menengah mengenai peluang melanjutkan pelajaran ke peringkat lebih tinggi. Majlis berkenaan turut diserikan dengan kehadiran Pengurus Besar Cawangan Maybank International Labuan, Nor Rashidi Mohammad, Pengarah UMSKAL, Prof. Dr. Shamsul Bahari Shamsudin dan Timbalan Pengarah Sektor Pembangunan Murid, Jabatan Pendidikan Wilayah Persekutuan Labuan, Imbran Yunus serta Ketua Bahagian Hal Ehwal Pelajar UMSKAL, Nur Iman Reedzal. Program itu dijayakan 40 pelajar Tingkatan 5 dari lapan buah sekolah menengah di Wilayah Persekutuan Labuan. Antara pengisian utama ialah sesi interaktif berkaitan saluran dan cara memohon ke institusi pengajian tinggi, termasuk Foundation/Diploma UMS, Matrikulasi, Form 6, Institut Perguruan Guru (IPG) dan Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET). Selain sesi motivasi dan perkongsian pengalaman, peserta turut dibawa melawat sekitar kampus UMSKAL bagi memberi gambaran sebenar kehidupan universiti. Dalam semangat tanggungjawab sosial korporat, pihak Maybank turut menyumbangkan dana kepada Dapur Siswa UMSKAL yang disampaikan Nor Rashidi kepada Prof. Dr. Shamsul Bahari sebagai inisiatif membantu pelajar B40 di kampus. Program ini menjadi platform strategik memperkukuh hubungan antara sektor korporat dan pendidikan tinggi, sekaligus menyemai semangat kesukarelawan serta kesiapsiagaan pelajar menghadapi masa depan yang lebih cerah.

title: Bursa Malaysia dijangka bergerak mendatar minggu ini
body: PETALING JAYA: Bursa Malaysia dijangka bergerak secara mendatar dan tidak menentu pada minggu ini dengan aktiviti penggiliran minat pelabur mengikut sektor. Remisier Maybank Investment Bank, Jeffry Azizi Jaafar berkata, tekanan utama terhadap pasaran dijangka datang daripada pendirian Rizab Persekutuan (Fed) Amerika Syarikat (AS) yang lebih ketat, peningkatan hasil bon negara itu serta pengukuhan dolar AS. Katanya, sentimen pasaran masih disokong harga minyak yang tinggi dan pemulihan saham semikonduktor di Wall Street. “Fed baru menaikkan kadar faedah, manakala hasil bon AS 10 tahun telah melepasi lima peratus, menyebabkan pelabur global lebih berhati-hati terhadap aset berisiko. “Justeru itu, Indeks Komposit Kuala Lumpur (FBM KLCI) dijangka bergerak dalam julat tertentu dan bukannya mencatatkan kenaikan menyeluruh. “Minat belian berkemungkinan tertumpu kepada sektor yang mempunyai pemangkin khusus, manakala saham berharga tinggi dan sensitif terhadap kadar faedah berpotensi mengalami pengambilan untung,” katanya kepada Utusan Malaysia. Beliau berkata, pergerakan ringgit, harga minyak dan aliran dana asing akan menjadi petunjuk penting kepada pasaran. “Penutupan positif Nasdaq pada Jumaat boleh membantu sentimen terhadap saham teknologi pada awal minggu, tetapi kenaikan hasil bon mengehadkan ruang kenaikan,” katanya. Mengulas lanjut, beliau berkata, sektor perbankan berpotensi menjadi antara penentu utama arah FBM KLCI minggu ini berikutan pemberatnya yang besar dalam indeks. Katanya, antara kaunter yang boleh diberi perhatian ialah Malayan Banking Berhad (Maybank), CIMB Group Holdings Berhad, Public Bank Berhad dan RHB Bank Berhad. “Jika bank-bank besar kekal stabil, FBM KLCI boleh bertahan walaupun prestasi keseluruhan pasaran bercampur. “Bagaimanapun, kenaikan kadar faedah AS tidak semestinya meningkatkan keuntungan bank Malaysia secara langsung kerana kadar domestik masih ditentukan oleh Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM),” katanya. Beliau berkata, dalam keadaan pasaran tidak menentu, sektor utiliti dan saham defensif turut berpotensi menerima pengaliran dana berikutan pendapatan yang lebih stabil. “Antara kaunter yang boleh diperhatikan termasuk Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB), Telekom Malaysia Berhad, Maxis Berhad dan YTL Power International Berhad. “Dalam pada itu, sektor minyak dan gas dijangka menjadi antara sektor paling aktif minggu depan berikutan harga minyak mentah Brent yang masih melebihi AS$100 (RM408.21) setong walaupun mengalami sedikit penurunan. “Keadaan ini dijangka mengekalkan minat terhadap kaunter minyak dan gas termasuk Hibiscus Petroleum Berhad, Bumi Armada Berhad, Dialog Group Berhad, Dayang Enterprise Holdings Berhad dan Velesto Energy Berhad. “Sektor ini mempunyai pemangkin paling jelas, tetapi pelabur perlu mengelak daripada mengejar harga sekiranya kaunter terus mencatatkan kenaikan mendadak pada pembukaan Isnin,” katanya. Sementara itu, Jeffry berkata, sektor teknologi dan semikonduktor berpotensi mencatatkan pemulihan secara terpilih selepas Nasdaq ditutup lebih tinggi pada Jumaat, dibantu saham semikonduktor. “Pelancaran global produk baharu Apple turut berpotensi mengekalkan perhatian terhadap rantaian bekalan elektronik. “Antara kaunter yang boleh diberi perhatian termasuk Inari Amertron Berhad, Malaysian Pacific Industries Berhad, Unisem (M) Berhad, Frontken Corporation Berhad dan ViTrox Corporation Berhad. “Bagaimanapun, sektor teknologi masih sensitif terhadap hasil bon AS. Oleh itu, kenaikan mungkin bersifat terpilih dan bukan semua saham teknologi akan meningkat secara serentak,” katanya. – UTUSAN

title: AG Cautions on Use of AI, Effective Human Oversight Is Still Essential
body: KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): While the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has been used extensively and relied upon in the last few years, Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar cautioned for the need for human oversight in its usage. Dusuki said there is no doubt that AI offers significant opportunities in various sectors. For instance, he said, in healthcare, it can assist clinical judgement while in the corporate sphere, it can support decision-making, improve efficiency, and help professionals process increasingly complex information. “But as our reliance on these systems grows, so, too, does the importance of understanding how they are used and how they are governed. We need to ask some very practical questions: How reliable is the information produced by an AI system? What are the limits of its capabilities? Who is responsible for checking its output?” he said. He questioned what would happen when the AI system does not perform as expected. “These are not merely questions about technology. They are questions of governance, professional responsibility, and human oversight. Increasingly, they may also have consequences for legal liability and insurance. “For any institution adopting AI, it is therefore important to understand why the technology is being used, what risks may arise from its use, and what safeguards are necessary. Technology may assist professional judgement, but effective human oversight remains essential,” he reminded. Dusuki was delivering his keynote address at the Inaugural Financial Lines Forum at a hotel here. Also present were Lembaga Tabung Haji chairman and RHB Bank founder Tan Sri Abdul Rashid Hussin, who delivered a special address, and former Federal Court judge Tan Sri Zainun Ali, former Chief Judge of Malaya Tan Sri Hasnah Mohamed Hashim, as well as former and current judges. The AG said that while there are continuing issues in the usage of AI, there is a need to use it responsibly. Dusuki said the use of AI requires engagement among those who develop the technology, those who deploy it, those who rely on it, and those who assess and manage the risks associated with its use. Hence, he welcomed the organisation of such a forum like the Financial Lines forum as it brings together legal professionals, healthcare practitioners, corporate leaders, insurers, brokers, and other stakeholders. “We have an opportunity to learn from one another, to better understand the risks and opportunities before us, and to consider how our respective professions can respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment. “Ultimately, the question is not simply what artificial intelligence can do. The more important question is, how we, as professionals, choose to use it responsibly,” he added. The one-day forum gathers medical experts, insurers, lawyers, and judges in exchanging views on medical negligence, governance, and AI. Meanwhile, in her welcoming address, Zainun, the chairperson for the Financial Lines forum, said a decision made in a boardroom may engage directors' duties, regulatory standards, disclosure obligations, and insurance coverage. “The adoption of AI in a hospital may raise questions of clinical judgement, patient safety, informed consent, data governance, institutional responsibility, and professional indemnity. “A claim may begin as a private dispute, but reveal a broader weakness in governance, documentation, communication, and risk management. No single profession has all the answers. Judges see how disputes crystallise and how legal principles operate in real cases. Regulators see patterns across institutions and markets. Lawyers advise on duties, responsibility, and remedy,” she said. Zainun added that directors and general counsel confront the practical demands of governance. “Doctors and hospital leaders carry responsibility for patient care. Insurers and reinsurers and brokers understand how emerging risks are assessed, transferred, and ultimately borne. “Sound risk management begins before a claim arises by identifying exposures, strengthening safeguards, and preparing for the consequences of loss. Risk professionals, insurers and reinsurers bring combined experience that can help institutions make informed decisions about the risks they accept, reduce, or transfer. The purpose of this forum is to place these perspectives in conversations with one another,” she said. The forum is organised by Messrs Chan Ban Eng & Co (CBE) where its managing partner, JJ Chan, is the founder of the Financial Lines forum. Chan said that he is pleased that Malaysia now has its own dedicated, pro bono Financial Lines forum, and he is proud to have founded it. “Financial Lines connects specialist questions of medical negligence, corporate and directors’ liability, insurance and reinsurance, and AI governance risk. Bringing these disciplines together can help improve patient care, strengthen governance, and deepen understanding of claims and coverage,” he added. title: Asteel lantik bekas Ketua Polis Negara Razarudin sebagai pengerusi selepas Clifford Hii ambil alih syarikat - Newswav
body: KUALA LUMPUR 7 Okt - Asteel Group Berhad melantik bekas Ketua Polis Negara Tan Sri Razarudin Husain @ Abd Rasid sebagai pengerusi bukan eksekutif bebas dan pemegang saham pengawal Datuk Clifford Hii Toh Leong sebagai timbalan pengerusi eksekutif, berkuat kuasa pada Selasa. Perubahan lembaga pengarah itu menyusuli penutupan tawaran pengambilalihan mandatori pada 5 Oktober yang menyaksikan syarikat pelaburan Clifford, Hii Capital Holdings Sdn Bhd, memegang 53.08% kepentingan dalam pengeluar keluli berkenaan. Clifford memperoleh kawalan pada Ogos menerusi pembelian 270 juta saham Asteel oleh Hii Capital, mewakili kepentingan 52.94%, dengan bayaran tunai RM20.25 juta atau 7.5 sen sesaham. Pembelian itu mencetuskan tawaran mandatori bagi baki saham pada harga yang sama. Jawatan Tan Sri (Dr) Soh Thian Lai ditukar daripada pengerusi eksekutif kepada pengarah eksekutif merangkap pengerusi emeritus, menurut makluman syarikat kepada Bursa Malaysia. Asteel turut melantik Esther Teh Oun Pheng dan Datuk Dr Lor Chee Leng sebagai pengarah bukan eksekutif bebas. Pengarah bukan eksekutif bukan bebas Christopher Hii Lu Ming serta pengarah bukan eksekutif bebas Yan Ying Chieh, Khor Hun Nee dan Wee Hiang Chyn meletakkan jawatan atas sebab peribadi. Pengalaman dalam keselamatan dan perkhidmatan kewangan Razarudin, 63, mempunyai pengalaman lebih empat dekad dalam keselamatan negara dan penguatkuasaan undang-undang. Ketua Polis Negara ke-14 itu bersara pada Jun 2025 dan turut berkhidmat sebagai pengerusi bukan eksekutif bebas Advancecon Holdings Berhad. Clifford, 43, mempunyai pengalaman lebih 20 tahun dalam sektor pendidikan, hartanah dan teknologi kewangan. Bekas pengarah bukan eksekutif bukan bebas HCK Capital Group Berhad itu mengasaskan Gambit Group Sdn Bhd dan pernah memegang jawatan pengurusan kanan serta menganggotai lembaga pengarah, dengan pengalaman meliputi strategi korporat, pembangunan perniagaan, urus niaga, pelaburan, tadbir urus dan pengurusan projek. Beliau ialah anak kepada bekas wartawan yang beralih menjadi ahli perniagaan, Tan Sri Clement Hii Chii Kok, pengasas dan pengerusi eksekutif pemaju hartanah HCK Capital serta pengarah urusan kumpulan dan pemegang saham utama kumpulan pendidikan swasta SEG International. Esther Teh, 47, mengetuai audit dalaman dan pengurusan risiko di Usaha Tegas Sdn Bhd serta merupakan pengarah bebas OMS Energy Technologies Inc yang disenaraikan di Nasdaq. Beliau mempunyai pengalaman lebih 20 tahun dalam audit, pengurusan risiko, perundingan, pelaksanaan perkhidmatan bersama, operasi dan kawalan kewangan. Jawatan terdahulunya termasuk ketua audit dalaman dan pematuhan kumpulan di Silverlake Axis Ltd, ketua pengurusan risiko dan jaminan bagi bahagian digital kumpulan di Petroliam Nasional Bhd serta pengurus kanan perundingan pengurusan di Accenture. Dr Lor, 62, mempunyai pengalaman lebih 35 tahun dalam perkhidmatan kewangan dan berkhidmat sebagai penasihat kepada Global ESG Leadership Organization serta Kementerian Ekonomi dan Kewangan Kemboja. Beliau pernah menjadi ketua pegawai eksekutif (CEO) dan pengarah eksekutif Canadia Bank PLC di Kemboja, CEO kumpulan EON Bank Bhd, pengarah bebas Mizuho Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, pengarah rumusan perbankan di Hewlett Packard Enterprise, ketua perbankan pengguna kumpulan di RHB Bank Bhd serta pengarah urusan perbankan pengguna di DBS Bank Ltd. - DagangNews.com
